title: Measure Review Time, Quality, and Cost
subtitle: Read a team-level scorecard and investigate the work behind the numbers.

sources.label: Microsoft Research · SPACE of Developer Productivity

scenes.title: Check what you are comparing
scenes.body: Use a common unit of work and report the sample sizes.
scenes.narration: The four-week pilot is complete. The manager brings forty eligible pull requests from the baseline and forty from the pilot. First confirm that both sets use the same eligibility and labels, and make any missing data visible. Pull requests are the unit for the scorecard. Repeated reviewer observations belong to one pull request. The results describe this fictional team's service during these two windows.
scenes.code:
Baseline: 40 eligible PRs over four weeks
Pilot: 40 eligible PRs over four weeks

scenes.title: Read queue time and effort together
scenes.body: The team waited less while the active review took slightly longer.
scenes.narration: Wait time is a queue measure. It fell from a median of eighteen to thirteen business hours, meeting the fourteen-hour target. Active review is the work someone spends inspecting a change. It went from twenty-four to twenty-six minutes and stayed within the twenty-seven minute limit. Tell this as two observations. The shorter queue is the measured benefit, and active review still costs people time.
scenes.code:
Median wait: 18 h -> 13 h | Target <= 14 h
Median effort: 24 min -> 26 min | Limit 27 min

scenes.title: Read the counts and the denominators
scenes.body: The rework rate rose above the agreed guardrail.
scenes.narration: Six of forty baseline requests needed material rework. Seven of forty pilot requests did, equal to seventeen and a half percent. That is above the fifteen percent ceiling. In this sample, all eighty requests merged and had the same follow-up period. Each group had one post-merge defect. Those counts are small. The manager reads the seven pilot rework cases and looks for patterns in the actual diffs.

scenes.title: Show what the cost measure includes
scenes.body: Use the same allocation rules and state what the total covers.
scenes.narration: The pilot ledger attributes a hundred dollars to licenses, twenty to remote workspace use for tests and CLI review, and a hundred and twenty to getting the team started. The total is two hundred and forty dollars. Across forty eligible requests, that is six dollars per request. Active review minutes are tracked separately in this scorecard. A future cost model can include labor with a clear allocation method.
scenes.code:
Licenses $100 + workspace $20 + training $120
Total $240 / 40 eligible PRs = $6 per PR

scenes.title: Inspect a sample of the rework
scenes.body: Check what happened in the actual changes and reviews.
scenes.narration: Read the pull requests and their review reasons. In four of the seven pilot rework cases, the proposed change touched files outside the ticket. That gives the manager and tech lead a concrete issue to discuss. Product telemetry may show that the team used suggestions. The pull request evidence explains where the review and rework happened. The team avoids drawing an individual performance conclusion from these counts.
scenes.code:
Sample: 4 of 7 rework cases touched extra files
Evidence: diff paths and review reasons
scenes.result: Next question: can tighter scope reduce rework?

scenes.title: Summarize benefit, limits, and evidence
scenes.body: Carry the failed guardrail forward into the decision.
scenes.narration: The scorecard records shorter median wait time and costs within the cap. It also records a quality guardrail miss, a small sample, and a historical comparison. That is enough to have a focused pilot decision. Share the team-level figures, definitions, and an example pull request. If a stakeholder asks whether the assistant caused the shorter wait, explain which parts of the process and staffing could also affect the estimate.
scenes.code:
Met: wait, active review effort, cost
Missed: rework ceiling
Monitored: defects and access incidents
scenes.result: Carry the scorecard into the decision meeting
